definition: Inequitable means unfair or unjust in how benefits and burdens are divided.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inequitable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inequitable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The settlement struck even the winners as inequitable: the families nearest the spill, who had lost the most, were paid the least.
Uneven is weaker than inequitable: an uneven split may have an innocent explanation, while inequitable asserts that the imbalance is unfair and should not stand.
Exploitative goes further than inequitable: an inequitable arrangement shortchanges one side, but an exploitative one is built to feed on that side's weakness.

Unjust condemns across the whole moral field — an unjust verdict, an unjust war, an unjust accusation. Inequitable is narrower and cooler: it points specifically at a lopsided division of benefits or burdens, the kind of unfairness an auditor can lay out in a table.
One-sided says the balance tilts — a one-sided trade, a one-sided match — without ruling on whether the tilt is wrong. Inequitable passes the judgment: the tilt is unfair and ought to be corrected.

The orchards at the canal's head — whose owners sat on the committee — drew water six days a week; the vegetable farms at the tail end, with twice the acreage and twice the workers, drew two.
The agricultural board's review needed only one word for the arrangement: inequitable.
Inequitable is not a complaint about mere difference — schedules can differ for good reasons.
It is the judgment that a division of benefits or burdens is unfair: advantage flowing to whoever controls the arrangement, need counting for nothing.
The word carries the cool authority of audits and rulings; it condemns the arrangement rather than the people running it, which is what makes it so useful in formal argument.
Inequitable is the language of audits, rulings, and policy briefs — a formal verdict that a division of benefits or burdens is unfair.
It judges arrangements rather than people: call the policy inequitable, not the clerk who applies it.
And keep it apart from a mere difference; paychecks tied to hours worked differ and are perfectly fair, and fairness is the only thing this word ever disputes.
